title: Jeremiah 46:1–12
context: Jeremiah introduces a collection of the LORD's words concerning the nations, which runs through chapter 51. Some Greek traditions arrange these oracles differently; see the note at 25:13. The first oracle concerns Egypt's army under Pharaoh Necoh, defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish by the Euphrates in the fourth year of Jehoiakim. In vivid poetry the LORD describes Egypt's troops preparing for battle, rising like the Nile, then fleeing in terror. The day belongs to the Lord, GOD of Armies, and there is no healing for Egypt.

verses.text: The LORD’s word which came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD’s word which came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations." Arminian readers see the LORD's rule extending beyond Israel. Jeremiah was appointed "over the nations and over the kingdoms" (1:10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this heading opens the oracles against the nations. The God of Israel is Lord of all peoples. Both traditions treat his rule over the nations as shared ground.

verses.text: Of Egypt: concerning the army of Pharaoh Necoh king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: "Of Egypt: concerning the army of Pharaoh Necoh king of Egypt." Arminian readers note the historical anchor: the battle at Carchemish "in the fourth year of Jehoiakim," when Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Pharaoh Necoh also appears in 2 Kings 23:29 and 2 Chronicles 35:20, where he killed Josiah. These notes name the connection without merging the accounts.

verses.text: “Prepare the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle!
verses.arminianNotes: "Prepare the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle!" Arminian readers hear the poem open with battle commands, as Egypt's army readies itself with confidence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the dramatic style: the LORD's oracle speaks as if giving orders to the army, only to show how its preparations will fail.

verses.text: Harness the horses, and get up, you horsemen, and stand up with your helmets. Polish the spears, put on the coats of mail.
verses.arminianNotes: "Harness the horses, and get up, you horsemen." Arminian readers see Egypt's full military strength on display, with helmets, polished spears, and coats of mail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the detailed preparations build tension for the reversal that follows. Human readiness cannot stand against the LORD's purpose. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and are turned backward. Their mighty ones are beaten down, have fled in haste, and don’t look back. Terror is on every side,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: "Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and are turned backward." Arminian readers see the sudden collapse of Egypt's mighty army, fleeing in haste as "Terror is on every side."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that "Terror is on every side" echoes a phrase found earlier in Jeremiah (6:25). The LORD himself declares the rout of Egypt's army.

verses.text: “Don’t let the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape. In the north by the river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen.
verses.arminianNotes: "Don’t let the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape." Arminian readers see that neither speed nor strength can save Egypt's soldiers when they stumble "by the river Euphrates."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal of human confidence. The swift and mighty are the very ones who fall. The LORD's purpose overrules military advantage.

verses.text: “Who is this who rises up like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge?
verses.arminianNotes: "Who is this who rises up like the Nile." Arminian readers see Egypt's ambition pictured as the Nile in flood, surging to overwhelm the lands around it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Nile, Egypt's source of life and pride, becomes the image of its arrogance. The question invites the answer given in the next verse.

verses.text: Egypt rises up like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge. He says, ‘I will rise up. I will cover the earth. I will destroy cities and its inhabitants.’
verses.arminianNotes: "Egypt rises up like the Nile." Arminian readers see Egypt's proud boast, "I will cover the earth," as the self-confidence that leads to its fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the arrogant claim, "I will destroy cities and its inhabitants." Egypt's pride sets itself up as a rival power to God's purposes.

verses.text: Go up, you horses! Rage, you chariots! Let the mighty men go out: Cush and Put, who handle the shield; and the Ludim, who handle and bend the bow.
verses.arminianNotes: "Go up, you horses! Rage, you chariots!" Arminian readers see Egypt calling on its allies, "Cush and Put" and "the Ludim," to join the battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Egypt's horses and chariots were famous. Isaiah 31:1 warns against those who "trust in chariots." Jeremiah's oracle shows that trust failing.

verses.text: For that day is of the Lord, GOD of Armies, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge himself of his adversaries. The sword will devour and be satiated, and will drink its fill of their blood; for the Lord, GOD of Armies, has a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates.
verses.arminianNotes: "For that day is of the Lord, GOD of Armies, a day of vengeance." Arminian readers see the battle as the LORD's own day of judgment on his adversaries, not merely a contest between empires.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the startling image of the battle as "a sacrifice in the north country." They compare Romans 12:19, "Vengeance belongs to me," where vengeance is left to God.

verses.text: Go up into Gilead, and take balm, virgin daughter of Egypt. You use many medicines in vain. There is no healing for you.
verses.arminianNotes: "Go up into Gilead, and take balm, virgin daughter of Egypt." Arminian readers see biting irony: Egypt, famed for medicine, uses "many medicines in vain." There is no healing for her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of Jeremiah 8:22, "Is there no balm in Gilead?" The same image used for Judah's wound now applies to Egypt. These notes name the link without merging the passages.

verses.text: The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for the mighty man has stumbled against the mighty, they both fall together.”
verses.arminianNotes: "The nations have heard of your shame." Arminian readers see Egypt's defeat becoming public, as the earth hears her cry and her mighty men stumble over one another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the mighty "both fall together." Strength collides with strength and collapses. The LORD's judgment exposes the weakness of every human power.
